_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 1 Computing unit lecture film, Lesson 5 Bugs and Debugging. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. The chapters follow LESSON['lecture'] in order (the first bug; run it to test it; find the bug; fix it and run again; everyone debugs) with the lesson's everyday-algorithm bug hunt (1CT.02) between the fix and the last part, in the lesson's own words: its moth story, its dog program right-left-jump with the bug in the second block, its block labels and colours from ART.block, and its own handwash scene (ART.scene 'handwash', built from a growing list of step ids). The wrong program is shown by passing the wrong list, never by drawing a separate picture of a mistake, and every cross in this film marks a step or a block, never a person.
title: Bugs and Debugging
subtitle: Grade 1 Computing
objectives: Predict what is likely to happen when programs are run.
Know that programs can contain errors.
Know how to run programs to test whether they produce the desired result.
Identify why a program does not produce the desired result.
Know that 'debugging' is the correction of errors in programs.
Identify single errors in algorithms that represent everyday events or tasks.

beats.say: A program can have a mistake in it. We call that mistake a bug.
Finding the bug and fixing it is called debugging.
Long ago, a computer was as big as a whole room.

at.room: as big as a whole room

beats.say: One day it stopped working, and nobody knew why.
Inside the machine, the people found a real insect. A moth!
People already called a mistake a bug. Now they had a real one!
They stuck the moth in their notebook. That story made the word famous.

at.stuck: stuck the moth in their notebook

beats.say: We want the dog to move right twice, and then jump.
Here is the program for it. Does it work? You cannot tell just by looking.
First say what you think the dog will do. Then press Run.
The dog moves right. Then it moves left. Then it jumps.
That is not what you said. So this program has a bug in it.
Why did it go wrong? Compare the program with what we wanted, block by block.
Block one says move right. We wanted move right. That one is fine.
Block two says move left. But we wanted move right.
Block three says jump. We wanted jump. That one is fine too.
So the second block is the bug. It says left instead of right.
Now fix it. Take the wrong block out and put the right one in.
Move right, move right, jump. That is what we wanted.
Now run it again. Always test again after you fix something.
The dog moves right, right, and jumps. The bug has gone.
You found the bug and you fixed it. That is what debugging means.
An everyday algorithm can have a bug too. Here is washing your hands.
Turn the tap on. Put soap on your hands. Then eat the soap?
Eating the soap does not belong here. That step is the bug.
Take it out. Rub your hands together instead, then rinse and dry them.
Sometimes a good step is just in the wrong place.
Rinsing before you rub washes the soap away.
Even expert programmers write bugs. Everybody does, every day.
A games maker tests her own game. A door will not open.
An app keeps closing by itself. The programmers send a fix.
A rocket's programs are tested again and again before it flies.
A bug is a mistake in the program, not in the computer.
Run it and watch it. Compare what happened with what you wanted.
Find the wrong block, fix it, and run it again. That is debugging.
